newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Slump expected in Carter Holt full year result.
newsitem.headline: Slump expected in Carter Holt full year result.

text.p: Low commodity prices and increased competition in packaging are expected to almost halve Carter Holt Harvey Ltd's annual profit to around NZ$235 million, (US$161 million) equity analysts said on Friday.
This would compare to last year's record profit of NZ$453 million but CHH is expected to maintain its total dividend at 10 cents per share.

While little had changed since the third quarter, when the company announced a nine-month profit of NZ$171 million against NZ$362 million a year earlier, analysts were cautiously optimistic for a pickup in commodity prices.
One key driver for Tuesday's result was expected to be the contribution from its 30.05 percent-owned indirect associate, Compania de Petroleos de Chile SA (Copec).
Progress on CHH's ambitious cost cutting programme would be another big factor, as would competition in domestic packaging from Visy, which is owned by Australia's Pratt Industries.
CHH planned NZ$30 million in cost savings in the year to March, NZ$75 million in 1997/8 and $100 million for 1998/9.
As always, pulp and paper prices would come into play, as would log volumes.
One analyst, who declined to be identified, said he was expecting a slightly higher outcome of NZ$240 million because he foresaw a greater contribution from Copec.
But he expected little change in the commodities outlook.
"While things are starting to look a bit better, there are still risks on the horizon," he said. "The fact is that pulp and paper is only a third of CHH's business," he said.
"Yes, there may be some recovery there, but more importantly is what is happening in their packaging and wood products businesses," he said.
Competition had forced CHH to ship more linerboard overseas, which meant lower margins and higher volatility.
Pulp prices, after the so-called "double dip", had recovered to similar levels experienced in the third and fourth quarters of calender 1996 of about US$580 a tonne.
"But it's a bit difficult to see whether this is a true market price or whether there are other some other peripheral factors at work there," John Cairns at Cavill White Securities said.
And while there had been progress in world inventory levels, he doubted they had reached equilibrium.
CHH, which is just over half owned by International Paper last year embarked on an 18-month NZ$313 million upgrade of its Kinleith mill in a bid to improve productivity.
